implementation_notes: Mockito is explicitly a Test Spy framework in its own FAQ: Mockito.spy(real) builds a proxy that delegates to the real instance, the test runs the SUT, then verify(spy).send(...) with times()/never() and ArgumentCaptor.forClass(...) assert what happened. What replaces the classic hand-written spy is the framework proxy plus the verification API; stubbing a spy requires doReturn(...).when(spy), and final classes, static methods and self-referencing real code stay outside its reach without inline agents.
pitfalls: when(spy.method()).thenReturn(...) invokes the real method while stubbing; use doReturn().when(spy) for spies.
Cannot spy on final classes or static methods, and spying on real methods that reference the outer class (OuterClass.this) is impossible - the FAQ lists these limits.
verify() compares arguments with equals(), so a mutable argument that changes after the call can fail against the recorded invocation.

variants.name: Hand-rolled java.lang.reflect.Proxy recording proxy
variants.implementation_notes: Where no mocking framework is allowed (or the collaborator is an interface you own), a dynamic proxy is the manual spy: Proxy.newProxyInstance builds the interface implementation at runtime and an InvocationHandler forwards to the real target while appending the Method and arguments to a list the test asserts on. What replaces the classic hand-written spy subclass is the reflective handler; it only works for interfaces and provides none of Mockito's matcher or verification sugar.
pitfalls: JDK dynamic proxies implement interfaces only; class collaborators need CGLIB/ByteBuddy-style subclassing, which Mockito already wraps.
method.invoke wraps the callee's checked exceptions in InvocationTargetException and boxes primitive returns, so the handler must unwrap and coerce or the SUT sees ClassCastException/wrong errors.
The call list is shared mutable state: synchronise it (or use a thread-local) when the SUT calls the collaborator concurrently.
